If this railway is not built up to the standard originally designed it will never be able to compete with the American seaports, because you cannot haul as many cars on a road with a 0.6 per cent grade as you can on a road with a 0.4 per cent grade. Our friends in St. John and Halifax were very greatly disappointed when the present Government took hold of the construction of this road. There is no evidence, in anything that has been presented in the report of Messrs. Gutelius and Staunton, to show that the money which has been expended upon this road has not been expended honestly.
There are on the other side of the House hon. members who are greatly disappointed with this report because the commissioners have absolutely failed to prove to the people that there is one cent of expenditure that has not been accounted for. These commissioners spent two years in an effort to find out if one cent has been misspent, but all they can say is not that there has been any wrongful expenditure, but that too much money has been spent. I can only say that we will have the very best road on the American continent and one that the people of Canada may justly be proud of.

Mr. Speaker, ever since the introduction of steam and railway travel in the world, and especially in America, it has been the 'laudable ambition of the people of the different provinces of Canada under the British flag to utilize the Atlantic ports which were placed there by the hand of Providence awaiting the further development of the western provinces and of our vast resources of soil, forest and -sea. While they were waiting, the necessity of bringing together those immense territories from ocean to ocean, which were to form the Dominion of Canada in the near future, and without the union of which no Canadian nation could have existed, impressed itself forcibly upon the minds of the people at that time. Without Atlantic ports, the old provinces of Canada would not have been able to rise to the position of a nation

because they would have been left for five or six months in the year at the whim of a collector of customs in the United States. The people of British and French origin were then all animated with the same desire to see the realization of the hope, which they had long indulged, of building up a united Canada and of shipping their products through a Canadian seaport. But, unfortunately, the Ashburton treaty was passed by the representatives of Great Britain and the United States, and Canada was left only the ports of St. John and Halifax, with their surroundings, which could be equipped as the future development of the country might require. Meanwhile the Intercolonial was constructed, and Halifax and St. John were placed in communication with Quebec and Montreal. Then, with the increase of population, the increase of traffic, and the vast development of the country, and its future being assured, the people of Canada decided, no matter what the cost, that they must endeavour to reduce the distance between the Atlantic and the Pacific, and decrease the cost of freight transportation between East and West, according to the dictates of the best science of the twentieth century. It was felt that no matter what the original cost, a first-class railway line should be constructed, by which, considering the lessened cost of operation, the people of Canada might have a reduction of, we will say, twenty-five per cent in the freight rates. I am not an engineer, nor a railway expert, nor even a lawyer, but I have heard the convincing speech of the ex-Minister of Railways, and I am able, without prejudice, to declare that he has demonstrated that the project formulated by the Liberal party in 1903 for the building of the Transcontinental railway, was a project in the best interests of the country, and a project which required some daring, and, in this age, Canadians must have daring if they are to progress. . I am not an engineer, but it does not require engineering skill to see that the report of Messrs. Gutelius and Staunton was not intended for the education, or edification, or enlightenment of railway engineers in Canada or elsewhere, but for the purpose of misleading the public. To-day we advance in a year as much as our forefathers advanced in a century; but Messrs. Gutelius and Staunton do not seem to realize that. The National Transcontinental railway was conceived in a spirit of patriotism, and one of its purposes was to effect a saving of twenty-five per cent
on the cost of transportation, and thus to add to the prosperity of the country. Mr. Gutelius, whom I have not yet met, seems endowed with a dual personality. There is Mr. Gutelius, of the National Transcontinental railway, who wants a transcontinental railway with heavy grades, and there is Mr. Gutelius, of the Intercolonial, who wants to strengthen all the bridges and to straighten out the curves on the Intercolonial railway, in order to save twenty-five per cent in the cost of operation, and for this purpose he is willing to spend $2,000,000 on 200 miles of road, an expenditure representing $18,000,000 for the Transcontinental. The Conservative party always want some kind of cry to delude the people; a few years ago, in Drummond-Artha-baska, they proclaimed that the Liberals wanted to send the children of the people as food for bullets in different parts of the empire, and now their cry is that millions of dollars have been wasted in extravagance by the late Government. I hear the hon. member for Peterborough make some remark, but I am sure he will agree with me that this report of Messrs. Gutelius and Staunton was not intended for the intelligent citizens of Peterborough, who know more about railroads than ever this report will teach them, but that its intention is to mislead others, who probably may not be so intelligent. I take a most serious view of this question, and so I wish to put on 'Hansard' some of the more salient paragraphs in this report, to show that tne intention was to mislead the electors into believing that there was extravagance in connection with the construction of the Transcontinental railway. It is very annoying for a true Canadian to have to read such campaign literature as is found in this report, and it is sad to think that two men could be found in Canada who would be guilty of such political animosity as the report shows these gentlemen were inspired with. Mr. Gutelius and Mr. Staunton may be all right as private citizens, but in making this report they were undoubtedly carried away by biased judgment and by political prejudice. Let me now read from the report a few extracts which I wish to put before the country .and which will be cited to the people of Canada. Take the following paragraph on the constitution of the commission :
Until the appointment of Major R. W. Leonard, in the autumn of 1911, no member of

the commission had any experience or knowledge of railway building or operation.
These words might lead laymen to believe that there was something wrong, .because the members of the commission had no engineering knowledge; but that point has been cleared up by the speakers who have preceded me. Those members of the commission had engineers to direct them in matters relating to engineering construction. They had the best engineers the country could produce-Mr. Lumsden, Mr. Gordon Grant and Mr. M. J. Butler, who a year or two afterwards .became Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals, whose knowledge of engineering cannot be denied by any one in Canada. He is not surpassed in Canada, in fact, he is not surpassed in America, in regard to the construction and operation of railways. He is well known and admired by everybody for his talent as a railroad constructor and a railroad operator on other lines to which he has been attached. As regards the chairman of the commission, hon. members from Nova Scotia could speak more eloquently of Mr. F. B. Wade than I could myself. Everyone who was in this House in the early years of this century and who knew Mr. Wade, knows that he was an honest man, with great knowledge and experience in the construction and operation of railways in .western Nova Scotia.
Hon. gentlemen opposite have' referred also to Mr. Parent. He has been connected with great enterprises in Quebec; not only so, but before he was on the commission, he was for several years mayor of Quebec. During his two or three renewed terms of the mayoralty, he aroused the people of Quebec from their centuries of lethargy, and he was the cause of the great prosperity of that city to-day.
In regard to momentum grades, the report reads as follows:
Had momentum grades been adopted, as is the usual practice in high class modern railway construction-
I wish to call attention to these words, which to my mind are deceptive or are altogether wrong.
Had momentum grades been adopted, as is the usual practice in high-class modern railway construction, they would have in no way impaired the usefulness of the railway, or increased the cost of operation, or reduced its hauling capacity, and $6,200,000 might and should have been saved.
In regard to bridges, the report reads as
follows:
Had wooden trestles been used instead of train fill and steel structures, as was done by

the Grand Trunk Pacific on its portion of the line, and as is allowed in the best modern railway construction, they might have been in course of time replaced by fill and steel structures and $2,947,227 thereby saved without impairing the usefulness or reducing the hauling capacity of the railway or increasing the cost of operation.
In regard to train filling, the report says:
The commission had an offer from the Grand Trunk Pacific to fill wooden trestles at the rate of 25 cents per cubic yard. Had the commission made such an agreement to do the train filling after the road was opened, $3,250,000 would have been saved in addition to that included under the last heading.
In regard to the method of inviting tenders, the report says:
The rules adopted by the commission in advertising for tenders, the unlimited security required to be furnished by the contractors, and the proposal to let the work for the most part in unreasonably large sections, resulted in only five contractors tendering for 806 miles of the railway, and eleven contracting firms secured all the work and sub-let it to upwards of 100 sub-contractors, who, had the work been divided into reasonably large sections and the security required in other Governmental contracts only been exacted, would have in all probability competed in the bidding. As an indication of the handsome profits derived by these eleven firms, it appears that they were paid $8,800,000 in profits fon that part of the work which they let to sub-contractors.
I will read the chief paragraph of the report on the New Brunswick section, as follows:
Large sums of money in interest have been lost by the premature construction of the New Brunswick section of the railway. In our opinion this section should not have been constructed at all. If one-third of the money had been expended on the Intercolonial railway it would have provided all the trunk line facilities for the province of New Brunswick which would be required for very many years.
In conclusion, the report says:
We find that the Transcontinental Railway Commission, the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, and those having charge of the construction of the railway, did not consider it desirable or necessary to practise or encourage economy in the construction of this road.
We find that without including the money which was unnecessarily expended in building the railway east of the St. Lawrence river. $40,000,000 at least was needlessly expended in the building of this road.
This is the basis upon which these commissioners have framed their report, not for the education of the engineers of the country but for the purpose of catching the votes of the people of Canada at the next election. I am not an engineer nor a railway expert nor a lawyer; but it must be remembered that the country is not without authority from which the Canadian people can always find the best examples

for any large national undertaking which' any government may have constructed or may hereafter construct for the benefit of the people- I have as an authority a gentleman dear to me for many years, a true Canadian and a true Britisher, a man who has lived perhaps fifty years in advance of his time, but who has for many years enjoyed the respect, the admiration and the gratitude of the Canadian people, a man whom I am pleased to describe as a bright illustrious engineering genius, whose authority in the minds of the people of Canada will certainly be accepted in preference to the authority of Mr. Gutelius or Mr. Lynch-Staunton, or both of them, a man who had at heart the future interest of Canada, and of Great Britain as well. I refer to Sir Sandford Fleming. He is a man imbued with the desire for the good of his country, respected throughout Great Britain as well as in Canada whom Providence seems to take pleasure in preserving to an old age to enjoy the admiration and gratitude of the people of Canada.
That gentleman has left a lesson for Canada, a lesson which could have been studied to advantage by the gentlemen who are appointed as inquisitors into the construction of this railway. Sir Sandford Fleming was appointed chief engineer of the first great national railway undertaking of this country. I propose to read from his own writings to show his principles, - theories and methods. I am sure that when I bring before hon. members the views of this great engineer none will be able in their heart of hearts to approve the Gutelius-Staunton report. The appointment of Sir Sandford Fleming to the position of chief engineer of the Intercolonial was made by a Conservative government, was made by Sir John Macdonald himself in 1863, an appointment immediately sanctioned by the governments of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia and approved "by the Government of Great Britain with praise to Sir John Macdonald for choosing a man of such ability. The commissioners of that day wanted to build the Intercolonial about of the quality of that approved for the Transcontinental by Messrs. Gutelius and Lynch-Staunton. Sir Sandford Fleming had to contend against that. He had to come up from New Brunswick and Nova Scotia and plead before Sir John Macdonald for better conditions . of the road; plead with him not to allow the construction of wooden bridges and momentum grades but to have masonry for substructures and iron for superstructures, thus having permanent construction, instead of having to renew every seven or eight years. Sir Sandford Fleming wanted a railway worthy of the Canadian people and worthy of the country's
10 p.m. great future. Let me read a few-paragraphs from the work of Sir Sandford Fleming entitled, ' The Intercolonial: A Historical Sketch.' It is too bad the American engineer appointed to investigate the Transcontinental had not studied this work for his own edification before he took the job of making his report. First, I will give Sir Sandford Fleming's theory about the bridges:
One important point on which a serious difference of opinion arose was in regard to the bridges. In the specification submitted by the chief engineer to the Privy Council the abutments and piers were designed to be constructed of the best description of masonry with iron superstructure. It appeared to the chief engineer that great precautions should be taken with these structures to have them permanent. Iron and stone being the most durable materials, their use would remove risk of accident from fire, and from natural decay. And, although the first cost might be greater, the permanent structures would avoid the constant periodical charge for restoration which wooden work would require.
Then, later he said:
In January, 1869, the chief engineer made his first appeal in the matter, to the Premier, Sir John A. Macdonald, and he submitted at length the arguments why iron and not wood should be used. This letter was referred to the commissioners in the usual course. It has never been replied to; and the arguments advanced in that communication remain to this day without refutation. But the decision of the commissioners was sustained. Five of the bridges were however, exempted from the principle originally laid down by the commissioners ; otherwise, the order was given that all the bridges should be built of wood.
And further on he says:
He cited two instances of bridges on the Grand Trunk railway, under the management of Mr. Brydges, having been destroyed by fire but a few weeks before the date of Mr. Brydges' statement. Mr. Fleming contended that his estimates were correct, and challenged examination into their accuracy; and he further made a final appeal in favour of iron bridges.
After an examination which established that the estimates of the chief engineer were correct, the commissioners eventually withdrew their objections and recommended that all bridges over 60 feet span should be built of iron. But the chief engineer persisted in his efforts to have every bridge, down to the smallest span -24 feet-made of iron, and at last, by an Order in Council dated May 12, 1871, authority was given to have them so constructed.
With the exception of three structures built of wood by direction of the commissioners, against the protest of the chief engineer, all the bridge spans, of whatever width, throughout the line, have the superstructure of iron.
In another chaipter, writing on the engineering character of the line, he speaks

first of the climatic conditions of Canada- which, however, seem to have been forgotten or put aside for the preparation of the Gute-lius-Staunton report.
The climate of Canada has a marked effect on railway works. The frost is very severe; it penetrates the ground, where denuded of snow, to a depth of from three to four feet, occasionally even to a greater depth.
He makes a distinction between a national undertaking and a private undertaking, and gives the reasons why in the latter the work should be of high grade. Here is the opinion of Sir Sandford Fleming on this great question:
No portion of railway work is more important than its bridges. When a line is carried out by private effort, a circumscribed capital may compel the adoption of cheap structures.
I call the attention of hon. gentlemen opposite to these words:
When a line is carried out by private effort, a circumscribed capital may compel the adoption of cheap structures. In some cases it is not the character of the structure, or its economy, which commends itself; but it is the necessity of the case, which limits the cost. A railway constructed to meet a national requirement, and situated like the Intercolonial, is controlled by no such limitations.
These words of Sir Sandford Fleming were used in reference to a national construction for Canada forty-five years ago, and to-day, when the necessities of the development of the West, which cannot progress any further without the winter ports of St. John and Halifax, are such that the people of Canada find themselves faced by the necessity of uniting the Pacific coast with the Atlantic coast by the shortest route possible for the great trade of Canada, they are more applicable than ever, much more than they were forty-five or fifty years ago. But Sir Sandford Fleming is a man who has lived fifty years ahead of his time, and his reasoning to-day should command attention, respect and the adoption by the engineers as well as the laymen of Canada.
A railway constructed to meet a national requirement, and situated like the Intercolonial, is controlled by no such limitations. It requires no argument to establish that in such circumstances all structures should be of the best form suggested by experience, and that the most durable material should be used. They are then permanently built, and require no subsequent renewal. The first expense is the one cost and in the end the durable structure is by far the least costly.
This is the basis of my remarks to you and to this House on this great question, which captivates to-day the attention not only of every hon. member in this House

but in the whole Dominion of Canada. I say that to-day, when the Government undertake to build a railroad or a canal, the people of Canada, the people of Ontario *-as the Government are undertaking to build a new Welland canal-do not expect that they will again build a nine-foot or ten-foot canal. This Government to-day is engaging in the improvement of the Welland canal at an expense of $60,000,00(1 or $75,000,000, an improvement which will be as much an advantage to the American people to the south as to the people of Canada or of Ontario, because it will only benefit the people of Ontario, it will not benefit the people of the Maritime provinces by the Atlantic coast. But I, as a Canadian, will never be influenced by sectional considerations, and I, from the north shore of New Brunswick, would vote with pleasure the $60,000,000 or $70,000,000 which may be required to complete the Welland as well as the Georgian bay canal. We will contribute our portion with pleasure, because the prosperity of one part of Canada will be the prosperity of their neighbours, and the wealth of a neighbour does me no harm. It is only by such patriotic and national considerations that we can expect to make Canada what it is destined to be by the end of the twentieth century.
I wish to call the attention of the members of this House to the distinction drawn by Sir Sandford Fleming between a national and a corporation undertaking. I listened with close attention to the address of my hon. and intelligent young friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen), a young man who has no more sincere admirer of his ability and his skill as an orator than the member for Gloucester. At the same time, while he has shown great facility in argument and figures, I am sure that the people of Canada and the farmers of the West who read his speech will be lost in its labyrinth of subtleties. They will require heavenly revelation to guide them through this labyrinth of figures and subtlety of argument, and I am sure that Providence is not prepared to extend to Messrs. Gutelius and Staunton that heavenly revelation, because they do not deserve it. It has been said and repeated in this House that the Canadian Pacific and the other companies, the Grand Trunk Pacific itself on the branches they are building, have used what he calls wooden bridges, wooden trestles, momentum grades. The people of the West know what happened in the case of the construction of the

Canadian Pacific railway. The Canadian Pacific railway was the first railway built through that country and it was built by the money of the people of Canada to as great or even a greater extent than has been the case with the National Transcontinental railway, which will remain the property of Canada. But in the building [DOT]of the Canadian Pacific railway as in the building of all corporation-owned railways through a new country, the road was built as cheaply as it could be done. Then, as years went on, they rebuilt the road again and again, having the people of the West to draw on in the increase of their freight rates. The people of the West have complained that they were being bled through their freight rates in order that the railway might rebuild its line every seven or eight years. At last they made it a perfect line, which will now afford much cheaper transportation, but the people of the country have paid for it. The people of the West have paid for the improvements from the Great Lakes to the Pacific coast. I say that without prejudice to any company, either the Canadian Pacific railway, the Canadian Northern railway or the Grand Trunk Pacific. They have succeeded through the people of Canada using their roads and paying the rates. Railway experts'state that 90 per- cent of the reductions in rates that have taken place in the last ten years have been due to the coming of the Canadian Northern railway. These reductions represent a saving in ten years of $17,000,000 to the farmers of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, and all that is the result of competition. For fifteen years the people of those provinces have been paying enormous freight rates to enable the Canadian Pacific railway to become the gigantic railroad that it is today. It i3 rich by reason of the money paid by the people of Canada in freight rates. Whenever a company has built a line, whether- trunk or branch, and has not had people to draw upon, it has failed in its purpose. If our branch roads in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, built in the early years of Confederation by small capitalists who could not afford to put their road in a good position, have not been improved, it is because the surplus revenue from passenger land freight traffic has all been used in maintenance, filling up the same holes every spring and keeping the road together. If we had built a road such as Messrs. Gutelius and Staunton suggest in their report, it would have been in the position of those Maritime railroads to-day.
If another authority is needed, I may cite Mr. Gutelius himself. Take the Intercolonial railway Gutelius. He wants to improve the Sydney branch of the Intercolonial, and is asking for authority to carry out a survey in order to improve that section. Let me read a newspaper clipping on this point:
The Minister of Railways, Hon. Frank Cochrane, has authorized a survey of the Intercolonial from Moncton to Halifax and Sydney, with a view to eliminating the present heavy grades, replacing light bridges with heavier steel structures, and finding out the cost and feasibility of a cut-off at Truro. The authority for carrying out the survey was given to General Manager Gutelius by the minister on February 2 last.
Mr. Gutelius, in his memorandum to the minister on the subject, states that by reducing the grades to a maximum of six-tenths the tonnage on the trains could he doubled, and by increasing the strength of the bridges, heavier motive power could be used on this section of the line. At present the maximum train between Sydney and Point Tupper is 540 tons. If the proposed improvements are carried out, the road could handle a train of 1,600 tons.
Mr. Gutelius says: * That would enable us to handle the Sydney business at less than half the present cost of transportation, and would reduce the total operation cost by twenty-five per cent.'
So says the Intercolonial railway Gutelius. He wants a couple of million dollars to improve the Intercolonial railway between Sydney and Truro, -a distance of [DOT]about 200 miles. If I am wrong in the distance, my hon. friend from Richmond (M,r. Kyte) will correct me.
280 miles.

At that rate $1,000,000 per hundred miles, he would want .about $18,000,000 to put the whole of tne Transcontinental in the same condition as the branch line between Sydney and Truro; and yet he talks about extravagance. He says money has been spent which need not have been spent for some years; but the farmers of the West need an efficient railroad now. The prosperity of our farmers depends upon a reduction in freight rates. A farmer is wealthy or poor according to the rate he has to pay to get his goods to market. To-day other men, besides Messrs. Gutelius and Lynch-Staun-ton, are giving their attention to the question of freight rates.
It is a national issue

It is a great national issue to-day. Men, to-day, in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, are giving their attention to the best means of securing reduced freight rates and cheaper transportation for grain. They are talking not only of the Georgian Bay canal, not only of the Welland canal, not only of the Hudson Bay railway, but they are talking of connecting the Saskatchewan river by a system of canals with navigation on the Great'Lakes so that their grain may be transported by water from the prairies of the far west to its market. You are aware, Mr. Speaker, that the Government of Saskatchewan have taken up this question. The Government of Saskatchewan appointed a commission a year ago to study this important problem and they sent commissioners to England, France and Germany in order that they might consider means for further reducing the cost of the shipment of grain from the farms in the West to the markets of Great Britain, France and otheT countries. While we hope that they may be able to work out a practicable system of canals we must not forget that our country cannot get along with canal transportation alone owing to our climatic conditions and to the fact that in many parts of Canada we have winter for five or six months in the year. Then our canals are of no use and it is to railway transportation that we must look in order that the grain may be forwarded to its ultimate destination regularly throughout the year. It is not enough that the grain shall be rushed through to the markets during the months of October and November, thus reducing the price to the farmers of the West, but it is necessary that we shall make provision to keep transportation going on the whole year round, winter as well as summer, so as to enable the farmers to take advantage of the market as well as the possible reduction in freight rates.
The hon. gentleman who spoke last (Mr. Davidson) made reference to a suggestion that the road should have been built as far as North Bay only. I would like to have seen the hon. the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) in the House when this pronouncement was made. I would have liked to have seen hon. members from the province of Quebec, and especially from Quebec city and west of that point, as well as hon. members from northern Ontario who are expecting a great development to take place in the districts represented by them, and I would like to have heard their comment upon this proposal. The hon. the Post-

master General, hon. members from Quebec and the Conservative papers of Quebec are to-day extolling the Government for the works and improvements they are carrying on in and around Quebec and the money they are spending in order to promote the prosperity of the people of Canada generally and of that district in particular. I would ask, if, without the energy, activity and patriotism of the right hon. leader of the Liberal party (Sir Wilfrid LaurieT), the northern part of Ontario and of Quebec would enjoy the prospect of prosperity which presents itself to their view to-day. I would like to ask you if the right hon. leader of the Opposition had not been seconded, fortified and assisted as he was by men of the highest standing from the province of Quebec and from all over this country, such as Sir Charles Fitzpatrick and others, he would have been able, by the inauguration of this great national project, to ensure the prosperity of Quebec while at the same time benefiting the country at 'large. While the National Transcontinental railway shortens the distance between Winnipeg, St. John and Halifax, and while it develops the portion of the country through which it passes, it at the same time contributes to the welfare of Canada as a whole. I really cannot understand how people, especially from the province of Quebec, should not be most pleased because, by the exercise of his ingenuity and talent, my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition has been able, while finding a means of enhancing the prosperity of Canada as a whole, to promote the prosperity of the people of northern Ontario and Quebec in particular. Simultaneously with the progress of other parts of Canada, Quebec is progressing and is becoming a great shipping port, which prosperity it would have lost but for the policy pursued by my right hon. friend. My right hon. friend realized that this great port of the province of Quebec was declining in public opinion, particularly among the commercial and shipping interests of Great Britain, who were insisting that all the trade should pass through the port of Montreal, and he has been able to retrieve the position of the port of Quebec, while at the same time benefiting the country generally. As a result of his policy, he has been able to make the port of Quebec what it is to-day, and our friends on the other side of the House should not have a word to say about fraud or extravagance because, but for the policy which has been

pursued, the stagnation which at one time characterized that port would have still existed.
That great man, Sir George Ross, who has been called away at a time when still greater services were expected from him by hiis fellow-countrymen, built the Northern Ontario and Temiskaming railway, and this was one of the causes of the defeat of his Government in 1903 or 1904. Yet, nothing has contributed more substantially to the prosperity of the province of Ontario than the construction of that public work. It has proved one of the greatest sources of revenue for the Whitney Government, and without it that Government would not be able to show a surplus at any time. This road was built into a part of the country which the opponents of Sir George Ross at the time declared to be of no value whatever, but which has proved to be of more value than any other part of that province, although it is only at the beginning of its development. Yet the critics of the Government of the day declared that the road should never have been built. Now, it is proposed by hon. gentlemen opposite that the National Transcontinental railway should stop at North Bay or Toronto. I would like to read to the House an extract from an article in the Montreal Gazette which was published a few days before the report of this commission was brought to the attention of the people of Canada. It is worth reminding the people of Canada how a man can speak the truth when he removes himself from political prejudices, and so I quote this article from the Montreal Gazette:
On the line of the Transcontinental there are some 230 bridges, the length of which would he, if all the spans were put together, 11 miles; weighing 61,000 tons : and costing 36.000.000. Among the bridges that span the Winnipeg river is one 300 feet in length. The Salmon river bridge, in the east, took 1,0S9 tons of structural steel.
The heaviest structure on the eastern division is the Little Salmon river viaduct-4,000 feet long, 200 feet high, and requiring 6,996 tons of structural steel.
The fact that 230 bridges were necessary in connection with the building of the Transcontinental gives a realizing notion of the truth of the saying that Canada is a country of distances.
The line passes over some of the largest and finest waterways in the world.
The bridge building in this connection has been carried out without accident-a record of note, considering the difficult nature of the work, the height in many cases and the rigours under which, in the winter, a considerable amount of the work was carried out.
An official description of the bridges and the difficulties encountered in the erection of them,
together with the nature of the country through which the line passes, has been prepared by the engineers engaged on the work and is full of fascination to those who are able to feel the interest and daring and heroism involved in such a vast undertaking-all- the work upon which was undertaken and carried out by men who, in risking their lives and suffering of all kinds of hardships, did not think they were doing anything beyond the day's work.
' And the day is not far distant,' said an official of the Grand Trunk Pacific, ' when the most desolate wilderness through which the line passes, will he composed of thriving communities. For that is the history of railways everywhere. And it will be the history of this great Transcontinental line, which, begun with misgiving, is to fill a largo place in our life and history. The need will declare itself more and more-all the time. That it. is to fill a large space Is proved by the energetic manner in which the Canadian Pacific railway is strengthening its position in the country, both east and west. That shows that it recognizes and provides for formidable rivalry.'
The Transcontinental Tailway will make of this wilderness, in northern Quebec and Ontario, the richest and wealthiest part of Canada, -wherein our people will live in happiness in the centuries to come. Out friends opposite have the hardihood to say that money has been wasted on this road, when that money has been spent simply to make the road as perfect as possible. Messrs. Gutelius and Staunton report that the portion of the road between Quebec and Moncton never should have been built, but would they say that the. section north of Ontario and Quebec never should have been constructed, -and that this fertile country should be left a wilderness? But for the patriotic foresight of Sir Wilfrid Laurie-r and -his supporters, the wilderness in northern Ontario and Quebec would not have been developed, and a wilderness it would remain for possibly another century. I assert, sir, that the time is not far distant when the winter ports of Halifax and St. John will not be sufficient to accommodate the trade of the West. I ask hon. gentlemen opposite who come from the Maritime provinces what they think of that portion of the report which says that the road should not have been constructed through New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. What does my hon. friend from Kings-Allbert (Mr. Fowler) think of the suggestion of Messrs. Gutelius and Staunton that we should have nothing but the Intercolonial railway along the north shore of New Brunswick?

My hon. friend was quite ready in answering and asking questions when he was on this side of the House; but to-night he is silent.
I did not hear the hon. gentleman's question; will he please repeat it?

I do not think the people of the Maritime provinces would be satisfied if the Transcontinental railway were not extended so as to bring the fertile products of the West to the Maritime ports. Would my hon. friend oppose a road which means prosperity and increased population to New Brunswick, and which will bring the grain of the prairie provinces and the mineral resources of British Columbia to St. John and Halifax and other ports? We have the immense forests of British Columbia, and we have the immeasurable ooal fields of that province which the Conservative members from British Columbia do not appreciate as I do, and we want those products carried over the Transcontinental railway to St. John and Halifax. I am from northern New Brunswick, and if there is one man more than another whose selfishness might be aroused by the proposition to have another railroad in the centre of New Brunswick, instead of carrying all the freight over the Intercolonial past the doors of my constituents, I am that man. But the moment the Transcontinental railway was projected, and the moment it was said it would pass through central New Brunswick, then foT the sake of my province, and for the development of our resources, land the advancement of the interests of our people, I held up both hands in support of the project. Our population was around the borders of the province, along the Intercolonial from St. John to Fredericton, and from there to Edmundston, and we have there the centre of the province, with thousands of square miles of the best forests and every possible product. We have there immense virgin forests and water-powers of all kinds, which will cause to arise every possible industry all along the railroad. Would we have said to the people of Canada, ' We are losing our population and you must give us more representation because of that? We do not want any improvement if you give us representation without population. I take the ground that we should get population first and then we shall get representation. They say that we should have no railway construction in the Maritime provinces, and 
they quote the name of the late Mr. Blair. There is not a man in this House who is a more sincere friend of Mr. Blair than I. I admired him not only for his political sagacity, but for the justice he did to the people of my own town in a certain crisis. My town people and my country people still revere the name of Mr. A. G. Blair, as they did twenty years ago, when he sacrificed his political career for the sake of justice in the small town of Bathurst. At the very time of his resignation from the Government, no man in this House was so much devoted to that gentleman as I was, for the reasons I have given. But Mr. Blair, when as Minister of Railways and Canals he first visited British Columbia in 1898 or 1899, told the people of that province, at a banquet, that the tipie would soon come when Canada would have three transcontinental railways, and that that time could not come any too soon for him, I believe from the bottom of my heart that the only consideration which actuated that great patriot, statesman and politician, was his love for the Intercolonial railway and for St. John, which he represented; and he was afraid that the National Transcontinental railway might interfere with the progress and prosperity of the Intercolonial railway and of the port of St. John, which he had so much at heart. If the railroad, instead of being built to Moncton, had been built straight to St. John, so as to take the whole trade to that port, he would have acceded to its construction.
When the people of Canada have time to consider seriously, to digest, to ponder over the report, the speech of the exMinister of Railways and Canals, and other speeches made on this subject; when they look over the conditions of the country which are fast forcing themselves upon the notice of the Government and of the people, they will come to the conclusion that the members of this commission have issued an ex-parte report which does not commend itself to the attention of the best papers of the United States or of Great Britain either. I have not time to give quotations, but I have seen many papers in the United States censuring the report as made ex-parte, in star chamber, because the Liberal party were given no opportunity of proffering evidence of any kind. That kind of inquiry does not meet with the approval of the people of the United States or of a great many people of Great Britain. Although it has been said, and it may be true for a while, that this report may possibly affect the credit

of Canada in Great Britain, I trust in the intelligence of the people of Canada and of the people on the other side of the ocean that, when they consider seriously the vast distance between the two oceans1 and the political bias which has characterized this report, they will immediately come to>
the conclusion that, after all, as the report itself says, there has not been one dollar of graft in the construction of this road, which may have cost $181,000,000 or more. The commissioners in their report insist that the exact amount of interest which the company will have to pay will be $5,400,000 a year, -and they claim that this will affect the operation of the road. In the beginning of my remarks I stated that if the company does not operate the road, it will only be because the road has not been finished according to the terms of the agreement between the Government of Canada and the company. If the company operates the road, it will be operating a line which will be as advantageous as any other line, because, while the company may have $5,400,000 of interest to pay upon the large capital for the construction of the best road not merely in America but in tl)e world, it will have practically nothing to pay for the maintenance of the road, which is perfect in every respect, and it. will save in operation thousands of dollars every day, which will amply make up for that interest. It was with that object in view that Sir Sandford Fleming said that the more perfect a road, the greater the economy in its operation and in its maintenance.
He did not build such a road as Mr. Gutelius would have built. For while Mr. Gutelius might have saved $3,500,000 or $4,000,000 a year in interest on cost of construction, he would have provided a road on which every year millions would have had to be spent in maintenance, besides which there would have been the rebuilding of these bridges and the taking out of these momentum grades, at immense expense to the people. Sir Sand-ford Fleming believed in saving expense from the beginning. I have given you the principles and theory of this great man who, as I have said, has the respect of the people of Canada, a man who has helped on not only the prosperity of Canada but the unity of the empire.
As against the opinions of this engineering genius, as I may call him, we have the theories of a man who is not a Canadian, who has not a Canadian's ideas and aspirations, -a man who may be an honest man in his way and a good engineer, but 138
one who, judging from his report, will not be considered by the people of Canada a great engineer. Had he a reputation as an engineer, a reputation which he wished to preserve, he would not have put his name to such a report as this to go before the people of Canada and the world. If he had a reputation as an engineer, he sacrificed it for a mess of pottage at the hand of the Government in the form of a fee of $26,000, followed by $20,000 a year during the time he is 'loaned' by the Canadian Pacific railway to this Government. Think, Mr. Speaker, of a proposal of momentum grades under the climatic conditions of Canada for the transportation service of the great cities of Canada today, which are to be much greater in a few years. Thousands upon thousands of people will use this Transcontinental railway in the winter; many will come from the prairies and the cities of the West to greet their friends in the East at the Christmas and New Year season. We see the Postmaster General making every effort to have the mails which -are brought by steamers delivered as rapidly as possible in the great commercial centres. If this is needed to-day, what may we expect in twenty years? In twenty years we shall have a population that will require the best railway that civilization can offer. Who then would propose to have twelve or fifteen passenger trains a day passing over this route and the lives of these thousands of people subject to the peril of momentum grades in the winter season?
Oh, oh.

Hon. gentlemen may laugh and think this is a joke. But winter is a fact that remains in Canada-we have had it this season, certainly, as severe as any time within the last fifty years. The conditions that exist, and that will continue to exist, must be provided for. And when I find engineers whom I try to respect saying that on the route from Moncton to Winnipeg momentum grades should be a feature of a high-class railway, I cannot but feel that those engineers have sacrificed their reputations.
Let not our friends on the other side believe that I am afraid of public opinion on this question. In the first place, these investigating commissioners have not been able to report a single dollar of graft; and we know very well that had they been able to find a loss of even a thousand dollars in this way it would have been their greatest pleasure. But they were honest enough not to fabricate it when they did



not find it. I 'believe that the Liberal party has come out of this investigation stronger in public opinion than ever. This report shows that we have given the people the best road in America. The people know that that road, if not too much degraded, -between Quebec and La Tuque- will carry traffic at a rate to defy competition.
And should there be that 11 p.m. degradation of the road, it will be Quebec and the Maritime provinces that will suffer, though that road was built to afford protection for Quebec against the rivalry of Montreal and to save the trade of the Maritime provinces through the winter.
The hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Davidson) ventured the prophecy that not one Liberal member would come back from Nova Scotia after the next election.
Did he say that?

Yes. Why did he not say that not one Liberal member would come back from the province of New Brunswick either? In 1908 my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, (Mr. Hazen), who, I regret to see is not in his place, spoke at a meeting in Quebec. He was then Prime Minister of our province of New Brunswick, and in his speech he declared that not one Liberal member would come back from that province in the election then pending. A travelling agent who was present beard him and said:	What about Gloucester?
' Never mind Gloucester,' the hon. minister replied, 'not one member will come back;' yet nine came back, and only four of the friends of the hon. gentlemen opposite. I for one do not feel the results of this investigation or of this report. Meanwhile it is our duty to lay the Whole matter before the mass of the intelligent electors of the whole country. The engineers and great railway experts will not be affected by this report, and when this discussion is over and, after a little time, the people of Canada are able to ponder over that report and its consequences, they will turn against this Administration and its supporters, because they upheld such a report, by men who are biased, and had but two considerations-one a political consideration and the other, an engineer, whose mess of pottage was there before him. That engineer had so little Canadian aspiration that he worked for railway companies in Canada for ten years without taking out naturalization papers, and it

was only when he became a servant of the Government of Canada that, rather than sacrifice his position, his $26,000 or $20,000 a year and perquisites, he became a British subject. Hon. gentlemen opposite but two short years ago declared that it was disloyal and unpatriotic to send a bag of potatoes or a bushel of wheat to the United States-no truck or trade with the Yankees; yet they call in American engineers, and a body of men in Toronto who opposed reciprocity brought the stone for an immense building from the other side of the line. The Liberal party have nothing to fear but everything to hope from the result of this report of Messrs. Gutelius and Staunton. Mr. Staunton's political bias is well known; he would not contradict it himself. While he was still engaged in the making of that report as commissioner, he took part in the elections in South Bruce. The hon. the Solicitor General said that he had finished his report before he took part in that election; but it had not yet been made public, so that his interference in the election was quite unjustified.
I feel sure that when the people of Canada have seriously considered the false theories of railway construction advanced in the report and the advantages which the Liberal party has given to the people of the country at large, to northern Ontario, to northern Quebec, and to the Maritime provinces, they will say to Mr. Borden that he should never have made public that report, that he should have studied it more carefully before he allowed it to be circulated. I am prepared to give credit to the two commissioners for being fair enough not to place any findings of graft in their report, although I have no doubt that that was because they could not find any. Meanwhile it is the greater satisfaction to the people of Canada that on that commission there has been such an active political gentleman as Mr. Staunton, because it is well known in Canada and in England, where Mr. Staunton addressed people on the loyalty question and against American trade in 1911, that if there had been a dollar or a million dollars of graft he would have been only too glad to have exposed it to the people of Canada.
